newsitem.title: UK: Europe's appetite grows for famous Jamaica coffee.
newsitem.headline: Europe's appetite grows for famous Jamaica coffee.

text.p: The growth of Europe's gourmet coffee sector is fuelling demand for the famous Jamaica Blue Mountain coffee, regarded by many as the world's finest, importers say.

The market for the exquisite coffee, consumed mainly by affluent Japanese, is also growing rapidly in Australia, Hong Kong, Singapore and South Korea, said an official at the London-based Blue Mountain Coffee Ltd (BMC).
The company is the sole distributor for the Jamaican coffee to non-Japanese and U.S. markets.

"The demand for exotic coffee is developing in not just Britain but also in Italy, Spain, France and Belgium," said BMC company director Peter de Bryune. "The underlying cause is the growth in the boutique (coffee) market," he said in an interview.
BMC assumed the distributorship for unroasted Blue Mountain coffee in 1995 following the takeover of a British coffee firm Gordon Langford.
It also acquired Gordon Langford's brandname for roasted coffee -- Langford Brothers 100 percent Pure Jamaica Blue Mountain -- which currently are on sale in French and British supermarkets.
BMC distributes about 600 to 700 154-lb barrels of green Blue Mountain coffee a year mainly to Europe.
"We hope to build it up," he said. The company's key European markets are Belgium, France and the UK.
The company also hoped to develop the market for the Langford Brothers brand.
Gordon Langford had been selling Blue Mountain in Europe since 1978. Prior to that, the coffee had disappeared from the market for many years, as it was all shipped to Japan.

The Japanese are still the largest buyers of the Jamaican coffee, accounting for some 80-90 percent of the annual production of two million lbs. Total world coffee output is around 16.5 billion pounds.
"This year has been a wonderful crop, so it's somewhere over two million lbs," de Bruyne said.
Of the remaining 10-20 percent of production, 60 percent goes to the United States, 30 to Europe and the Middle East and the rest goes to South Korea and Singapore, he said.
Coffee connoisseurs call Blue Mountain, grown within a three mile radius of Blue Mountain peak on the southern end of Jamaica, the king of coffee.
The terrain, just under 5,000 feet (around 1,500 metres), possesses the ideal combination of soil, temperature, and water to produce a unique variety of the arabica coffee bean.
It carries a high price tag since it is very scarce and always in high demand. In London, a pound of Blue Mountain beans retails at 34 stg compared with 7.20 stg for Colombian coffee.

The unroasted coffee bean is a distinct bluish-grey colour. "It yields the finest cup of coffee, full bodied, medium acidity, very aromatic with a tinge of sweet bourbon-like taste," according to one coffee publication.
"It's the Rolls-Royce of coffee," de Bryune added. By itself it is a good coffee, even better by blending."
Importers said the supply scarcity has led to an active secondary market especially in Japan for Blue Mountain.
But de Bruyne said the trend was less rampant in Europe. The company deals only with main traders in each country who, in turn, sell to smaller roasters.
"To this end, we are holding our principal stocks in London with subsidiary reserves in Antwerp and Trieste," he said. The coffee is air-freighted from Jamaica to London.
-- Jalil Hamid, London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
